statement: Let $f$ be a [space-constructible function](c:space-constructible-function) with $f(n) \ge \log n$ and let $g(n) = o(f(n))$. Some language is decided by a deterministic [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) in space $O(f(n))$ and by no such machine in space $g(n)$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [space-constructible](c:space-constructible-function) and $f(n) \ge \log n$.
The function $g$ satisfies $g(n) = o(f(n))$.

conclusion: Some language is in $\mathrm{SPACE}(f(n))$ but not in $\mathrm{SPACE}(g(n))$, so $\mathrm{SPACE}(g) \subsetneq \mathrm{SPACE}(f)$.

proofs.name: Diagonalization
proofs.slogan: A machine $D$ simulates each machine $M$ on its own code within $f(n)$ cells and gives the opposite answer.
proofs.scope: The deterministic hierarchy theorem. The nondeterministic hierarchy theorem is another member of the family.

roles.why: Space-constructibility lets $D$ mark off $f(n)$ cells, and $f(n) \ge \log n$ leaves room for head positions and counters.
The relation $g = o(f)$ makes the simulation of a $g$-space machine fit into $f(n)$ cells for long inputs.

steps.slogan: Build a machine $D$ that marks off $f(n)$ cells and accepts only inputs of the form $\langle M\rangle 10^k$.
steps.detail: On input $w$ of length $n$, $D$ computes $f(n)$ and marks that many cells, which is possible because $f$ is [space-constructible](c:space-constructible-function). $D$ rejects unless $w = \langle M\rangle 10^k$ for some [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) $M$, and $D$ rejects if it ever needs a cell outside the marked cells.

steps.slogan: Simulate $M$ on $w$ inside the marked cells and count its steps.
steps.detail: $D$ simulates $M$ on $w$ and keeps a binary step counter of $O(f(n))$ bits. A machine of space $f(n)$ has at most $n f(n)\,|\Gamma|^{f(n)} \le 2^{d f(n)}$ [configurations](c:cfg), so $D$ rejects after $2^{d f(n)}$ steps. Hence $D$ always halts in space $O(f(n))$.

steps.slogan: Flip the answer of $M$ so that $D$ disagrees with $M$ on $w$.
steps.detail: $D$ rejects if $M$ accepts $w$ and accepts if $M$ rejects $w$; if the simulation is cut off, $D$ rejects. So $D$ decides a language $L(D)$ in space $O(f(n))$.

steps.slogan: Pad the code of $M$ so that the simulation of $M$ fits into $f(n)$ cells.
steps.detail: Suppose a machine $M$ decides $L(D)$ in space $g(n)$. Simulating $M$ on the fixed alphabet of $D$ takes $c\,g(n)$ cells, with $c$ depending only on $M$. Since $g = o(f)$, we have $c\,g(n) < f(n)$ and $M$ halts within $2^{d f(n)}$ steps for all large $n$, so $w = \langle M\rangle 10^k$ with $k$ large lets the simulation finish.

steps.slogan: Run $D$ on $w = \langle M\rangle 10^k$ to get a contradiction.
steps.detail: On $w$ the simulation finishes, so $D$ gives the opposite answer to $M$: $w \in L(D)$ if and only if $M$ rejects $w$. Then $M$ does not decide $L(D)$. This is the diagonal argument, so no machine of space $g(n)$ decides $L(D)$, while $D$ does so in space $O(f(n))$.

concepts.c:space-constructible-function: It lets the diagonal machine mark off exactly $f(n)$ cells.
concepts.c:turing-machine: The diagonal machine simulates other machines from their codes.
concepts.c:cfg: Counting configurations bounds the running time of the simulation.
concepts.c:asymptotic-notation: The relation $g = o(f)$ makes the simulation fit for large inputs.

source.note: The diagonalization of Stearns, Hartmanis and Lewis (1965); textbook form in Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, Section 9.1.

statement: Let $C \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a pointed [rational cone](c:rational-cone) of dimension $d$. Its [generating functions](c:generating-function) $F_C(x)=\sum_{m \in C \cap \mathbb{Z}^d} x^m$ and $F_{C^\circ}(x)=\sum_{m \in C^\circ \cap \mathbb{Z}^d} x^m$ are [rational functions](c:rational-function) and satisfy $F_C(1/x) = (-1)^d F_{C^\circ}(x)$.

hypotheses.text: The set $C \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ is a pointed [rational cone](c:rational-cone): the nonnegative span of finitely many integer vectors, with no line inside.
The cone $C$ has dimension $d$.

conclusion: The series $F_C$ and $F_{C^\circ}$ are rational functions, and $F_C(1/x) = (-1)^d F_{C^\circ}(x)$.

proofs.name: Triangulation and links
proofs.slogan: Prove the law for simplicial cones with a fundamental parallelepiped, then triangulate and sum over faces with Euler characteristics of links.
proofs.scope: The theorem for full-dimensional cones; a cone of dimension $k<d$ is treated in the lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d \cap \operatorname{span} C$ with $k$ in place of $d$. The identity is one of rational functions.

roles.why: Integer generators give rational series for simplicial cones, and pointedness gives a triangulation with a bounded cross-section.
Full dimension makes the link of an interior face a sphere of the right dimension, which gives the sign $(-1)^d$.

steps.slogan: Write the lattice points of a simplicial cone through a fundamental parallelepiped.
steps.detail: Let $\sigma$ have independent primitive integer generators $v_1,\dots,v_k$ and let $\Lambda = \mathbb{Z}^d \cap \operatorname{span}\sigma$. With $\Pi = \{\sum \lambda_i v_i : 0 \le \lambda_i < 1\}$, each lattice point of $\sigma$ is uniquely $w + \sum a_i v_i$ with $w \in \Pi \cap \Lambda$ and $a_i \in \mathbb{N}$. The [geometric series](c:geometric-series) give $F_\sigma = \sum_{w\in\Pi} x^w \prod_i (1-x^{v_i})^{-1}$; for the [relative interior](c:relative-interior) use $\Pi' = \{0 < \lambda_i \le 1\}$.

steps.slogan: Reflect the series of a simplicial cone and match the two parallelepipeds.
steps.detail: The map $w \mapsto \sum v_i - w$ is a bijection from $\Pi \cap \Lambda$ onto $\Pi' \cap \Lambda$. Since $(1-x^{-v})^{-1} = -x^{v}(1-x^{v})^{-1}$, we get $F_\sigma(1/x) = (-1)^k F_{\sigma^\circ}(x)$ for $k=\dim\sigma$. Replacing $x$ by $1/x$ gives $F_{\sigma^\circ}(1/x) = (-1)^k F_\sigma(x)$.

steps.slogan: Triangulate $C$ into simplicial cones on its own rays and split $C$ into open pieces.
steps.detail: A pointed cone has a [triangulation](c:triangulation) $\Delta$ into simplicial cones with no new rays (triangulate a cross-section polytope on its vertices). The relative interiors of the cones of $\Delta$ partition $C$, so $F_C = \sum_{\sigma\in\Delta} F_{\sigma^\circ}$ and $F_{C^\circ} = \sum_{\sigma^\circ \subset C^\circ} F_{\sigma^\circ}$. Also $F_\sigma = \sum_{\tau \le \sigma} F_{\tau^\circ}$ over faces $\tau$.

steps.slogan: Reflect every open piece and expand each closed cone into its open faces.
steps.detail: By step 2, $F_{\tau^\circ}(1/x) = (-1)^{\dim\tau} F_\tau(x) = (-1)^{\dim\tau}\sum_{\rho \le \tau} F_{\rho^\circ}(x)$. Summing over $\tau \in \Delta$ gives $F_C(1/x) = \sum_{\rho\in\Delta} F_{\rho^\circ}(x)\, c_\rho$ with $c_\rho = \sum_{\tau \ge \rho} (-1)^{\dim \tau}$, the sum over cones of $\Delta$ that contain $\rho$ as a face.

steps.slogan: Compute the alternating sum $c_\rho$ as an Euler characteristic of the link of $\rho$.
steps.detail: Cut $C$ by a hyperplane to get a triangulated $(d-1)$-ball $P$. For $\rho \ne 0$, $c_\rho = (-1)^{\dim\rho+1}\tilde\chi(\operatorname{lk}\rho)$, with $\tilde\chi$ the reduced [Euler characteristic](c:euler-characteristic): the link is a sphere of dimension $d-\dim\rho-1$ if $\rho^\circ \subset C^\circ$, giving $(-1)^d$, and a ball if $\rho \subset \partial C$, giving $0$. For $\rho = 0$ the link is $P$, so $c_0 = 1-\chi(P) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Collect the surviving terms to get $F_C(1/x) = (-1)^d F_{C^\circ}(x)$.
steps.detail: By step 5 only the faces $\rho$ with $\rho^\circ \subset C^\circ$ remain, each with factor $(-1)^d$. So $F_C(1/x) = (-1)^d \sum_{\rho^\circ \subset C^\circ} F_{\rho^\circ}(x) = (-1)^d F_{C^\circ}(x)$ by step 3. Both series are finite sums of rational functions, hence rational.

concepts.c:rational-cone: Its integer generators make every simplicial piece a rational series.
concepts.c:generating-function: The theorem compares the series of lattice points of $C$ and $C^\circ$.
concepts.c:rational-function: Each series sums to a rational function, which allows $x \mapsto 1/x$.
concepts.c:geometric-series: Geometric series sum the lattice points along each generator.
concepts.c:relative-interior: Relative interiors of faces partition the cone into open pieces.
concepts.c:triangulation: It splits $C$ into simplicial cones whose open faces partition $C$.
concepts.c:euler-characteristic: It evaluates the alternating sum over cones that contain a face.

source.note: Triangulation proof of Stanley's reciprocity theorem for rational cones; the simplicial case is a fundamental parallelepiped computation.

statement: Every [contraction](c:contraction-mapping) $T$ on a complex [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ has a [unitary](c:unitary-operator) dilation: a Hilbert space $K \supseteq H$ and a unitary $U$ on $K$ with $T^n = P_H U^n|_H$ for all $n \ge 0$.

hypotheses.text: The space $H$ is a complex [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space).
The operator $T$ on $H$ is a [contraction](c:contraction-mapping): $\|T\| \le 1$.

conclusion: There are a Hilbert space $K \supseteq H$ and a unitary $U$ on $K$ with $T^n = P_H U^n|_H$ for every $n \ge 0$.

proofs.name: Schäffer matrix
proofs.slogan: Fill the defect operators into a unitary block, then shift the rest of $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, H)$ so that powers of $U$ compress to powers of $T$.
proofs.scope: The existence of the dilation; the uniqueness of the minimal dilation is a separate part of the record and is not proved here. The scalar field is $\mathbb{C}$.

roles.why: The Hilbert space gives adjoints, positive square roots and orthogonal direct sums.
The bound $\|T\| \le 1$ makes $I - T^*T$ and $I - TT^*$ positive, so the defect operators exist.

steps.slogan: Define the defect operators and show that $T D_T = D_{T^*} T$.
steps.detail: Since $\|T\| \le 1$, the [positive operators](c:positive-operator) $I - T^*T$ and $I - TT^*$ have square roots $D_T$ and $D_{T^*}$. From $T(I - T^*T) = (I - TT^*)T$ we get $T\,p(T^*T) = p(TT^*)\,T$ for polynomials $p$, hence for continuous $p$ on $[0,1]$ by approximation. The choice $p(t) = \sqrt{1-t}$ gives $T D_T = D_{T^*} T$, and the adjoint gives $D_T T^* = T^* D_{T^*}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the block matrix $W = \begin{pmatrix} T & D_{T^*} \\ D_T & -T^* \end{pmatrix}$ is unitary on $H \oplus H$.
steps.detail: The products $W^*W$ and $WW^*$ have diagonal entries $T^*T + D_T^2 = I$ and $D_{T^*}^2 + TT^* = I$ (and the two similar ones). Their off-diagonal entries vanish by the two identities of step 1. So $W^*W = WW^* = I$.

steps.slogan: Build $U$ on $K = \ell^2(\mathbb{Z}, H)$ from the block $W$ and identity shifts.
steps.detail: Write the [direct sum](c:direct-sum) $K = \bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb{Z}} H_j$ with $H_j = H$ and $H = H_0$. Let $U$ map $H_0 \oplus H_{-1}$ onto $H_0 \oplus H_1$ by $W$, and map $H_j$ onto $H_{j+1}$ by the identity for $j \ge 1$ and for $j \le -2$. The sources cover every index and so do the targets, so $U$ is unitary.

steps.slogan: Follow $U^n x$ for $x \in H$ and read off its $H_0$ component.
steps.detail: For $x \in H_0$ we have $Ux = Tx + D_T x$ with $Tx \in H_0$ and $D_T x \in H_1$. Vectors in $H_j$ with $j \ge 1$ only move to higher indices. By induction, $U^n x = T^n x + y_n$ with $y_n \in \bigoplus_{j \ge 1} H_j$, so $P_H U^n x = T^n x$.

concepts.c:contraction-mapping: The norm bound $\|T\| \le 1$ makes the defect operators exist.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: It supplies adjoints, square roots and the orthogonal sum $K$.
concepts.c:unitary-operator: The constructed operator $U$ must be unitary on $K$.
concepts.c:positive-operator: Positive operators have square roots, which define $D_T$ and $D_{T^*}$.
concepts.c:direct-sum: The big space $K$ is an orthogonal direct sum of copies of $H$.

source.note: Schäffer's matrix construction of the unitary dilation; see Sz.-Nagy and Foias, Harmonic Analysis of Operators on Hilbert Space, Chapter I.

statement: Every language in the [polynomial hierarchy](c:polynomial-hierarchy) is decided by a deterministic polynomial-time [oracle machine](c:oracle-machine) that queries a $\#\mathrm{P}$ function: $\mathrm{PH} \subseteq \mathrm{P}^{\#\mathrm{P}} = \mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{PP}}$.

proofs.name: Toda's two inclusions
proofs.slogan: Put the hierarchy into BP$\cdot\oplus$P with Valiant-Vazirani and parity arithmetic, then derandomize with one amplified counting query.
proofs.scope: An outline of Toda's published proof; the cited paper proves each step in full. Steps 1 and 2 show $\mathrm{PH} \subseteq \mathrm{BP}\cdot\oplus\mathrm{P}$ and steps 3 and 4 show $\mathrm{BP}\cdot\oplus\mathrm{P} \subseteq \mathrm{P}^{\#\mathrm{P}}$.

steps.slogan: Reduce satisfiability randomly to formulas with an odd number of solutions.
steps.detail: The Valiant-Vazirani theorem gives a randomized polynomial-time map $\varphi \mapsto \varphi'$: if $\varphi$ is unsatisfiable, $\varphi'$ has no solution, and if $\varphi$ is satisfiable, then with probability at least $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ it has exactly one. Toda combines this with the closure of $\oplus\mathrm{P}$ under complement and polynomial disjunction to get $\mathrm{NP} \subseteq \mathrm{BP}\cdot\oplus\mathrm{P}$.

steps.slogan: Show by induction on the level that every class $\Sigma_k^p$ lies in BP$\cdot\oplus$P.
steps.detail: Toda relativizes step 1 and swaps the operators $\exists$, $\oplus$ and BP past each other at the cost of one more BP$\cdot\oplus$ layer, using that [BPP](c:bpp) is closed under complement and composition. Each level of the hierarchy then collapses into one layer, so $\mathrm{PH} \subseteq \mathrm{BP}\cdot\oplus\mathrm{P}$.

steps.slogan: Amplify the parity so that residues modulo a large power of $2$ separate yes from no.
steps.detail: A fixed polynomial with nonnegative coefficients, such as $q(y)=3y^4+4y^3$, maps $y \equiv 0$ and $y \equiv -1 \pmod m$ to $0$ and $-1 \pmod{m^2}$. Iterating it $O(\log n)$ times turns a parity count into a count that is $0$ or $-1$ modulo $2^{p(n)}$. The new count is again a $\#\mathrm{P}$ function, because $\#\mathrm{P}$ is closed under sums and products.

steps.slogan: Sum the amplified counts over all random strings with one $\#\mathrm{P}$ query.
steps.detail: Let $N(x,r)$ be the amplified count for input $x$ and random string $r$ of length $q(n)$, with $p(n) > q(n)$. The total $\sum_r N(x,r)$ is a $\#\mathrm{P}$ value, and modulo $2^{p(n)}$ it equals minus the number of strings $r$ on which the parity is odd. A polynomial-time machine reads that number from one oracle answer and compares it with the BP threshold.

steps.slogan: Combine the two inclusions and relate $\mathrm{P}^{\#\mathrm{P}}$ to $\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{PP}}$.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 2 put a language of $\mathrm{PH}$ into $\mathrm{BP}\cdot\oplus\mathrm{P}$, and steps 3 and 4 decide it in $\mathrm{P}^{\#\mathrm{P}}$. The classes $\mathrm{P}^{\#\mathrm{P}}$ and $\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{PP}}$ agree, since a $\mathrm{PP}$ oracle finds a $\#\mathrm{P}$ value by binary search and a $\#\mathrm{P}$ oracle answers $\mathrm{PP}$ queries.

concepts.c:polynomial-hierarchy: The theorem bounds the hierarchy; its levels are collapsed one by one.
concepts.c:oracle-machine: The final machine asks one oracle question to a $\#\mathrm{P}$ function.
concepts.c:bpp: Randomized error reduction keeps BP$\cdot\oplus$P closed under the level swaps.

source.ref: S. Toda, PP is as hard as the polynomial-time hierarchy, SIAM Journal on Computing 20 (1991), 865-877
source.note: Toda proves PH in BP.parity-P by Valiant-Vazirani and operator swapping, then BP.parity-P in P^#P by modular amplification.

statement: If a transversal crosses two [parallel lines](c:parallel-lines) in the Euclidean plane, then the alternate interior [angles](c:angle) are equal.

hypotheses.text: The lines lie in the Euclidean plane, where Euclid's parallel postulate holds.
The lines $\ell$ and $m$ are [parallel](c:parallel-lines): they lie in one plane and do not meet.
The line $t$ meets $\ell$ at a point $A$ and $m$ at a point $B$, with $A \ne B$.

conclusion: The alternate interior [angles](c:angle) that $t$ makes with $\ell$ at $A$ and with $m$ at $B$ are equal.

proofs.name: Euclid I.29
proofs.slogan: If the alternate angles differed, the interior angles on one side would sum to less than two right angles, so the parallel postulate would make the lines meet.
proofs.scope: The direct statement. The converse (equal alternate angles make the lines parallel) is Euclid I.27 and needs no parallel postulate.

roles.why: Two distinct crossing points $A$ and $B$ define the angles on both sides of $t$.
Parallel lines have no common point, which contradicts the meeting point from the postulate.
The parallel postulate says that the lines meet on the side where the interior angles sum to less than two right angles.

steps.slogan: Name the alternate angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ and the interior angles on one side of $t$.
steps.detail: Choose $C \in \ell$ and $D \in m$ on opposite sides of $t$, and let $\alpha = \angle CAB$ and $\beta = \angle ABD$ be the alternate [angles](c:angle). Let $C'$ lie on $\ell$ on the other side of $A$ from $C$. Then $\angle C'AB = 180^\circ - \alpha$ because two angles on a straight line sum to $180^\circ$.

steps.slogan: Assume $\alpha \ne \beta$ and compare the interior angles on each side with two right angles.
steps.detail: On the side of $D$ the interior angles $\angle C'AB$ and $\angle ABD$ sum to $180^\circ - \alpha + \beta$. On the side of $C$ they sum to $180^\circ + \alpha - \beta$. If $\alpha \ne \beta$, exactly one of the two sums is less than $180^\circ$.

steps.slogan: Apply the parallel postulate on the side with the smaller sum.
steps.detail: Euclid's parallel postulate says that, if the interior angles on one side of a transversal sum to less than two right angles, then the two lines meet on that side. So $\ell$ and $m$ meet.

steps.slogan: Contradict the parallelism of $\ell$ and $m$ to get $\alpha = \beta$.
steps.detail: The lines $\ell$ and $m$ are [parallel](c:parallel-lines), so they do not meet. This contradicts step 3, so the assumption $\alpha \ne \beta$ is false and $\alpha = \beta$.

concepts.c:angle: The theorem compares two angles that $t$ makes with the lines.
concepts.c:parallel-lines: Parallelism gives the contradiction when the postulate yields a meeting point.

statement: Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be bounded and open, $n \ge 2$. There are constants $\alpha, C > 0$ depending only on $n$ such that every $u$ in the [Sobolev space](c:sobolev-space) $W_0^{1,n}(\Omega)$ with $\|\nabla u\|_{n} \le 1$ satisfies $\int_\Omega \exp(\alpha |u|^{n/(n-1)})\,dx \le C|\Omega|$. So $u$ lies in an exponential [Orlicz space](c:orlicz-space).

hypotheses.text: The set $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is bounded and open, and $n \ge 2$.
The function $u$ lies in the [Sobolev space](c:sobolev-space) $W_0^{1,n}(\Omega)$ and $\|\nabla u\|_{L^n} \le 1$.

conclusion: The integral $\int_\Omega \exp(\alpha |u|^{n/(n-1)})\,dx$ is at most $C|\Omega|$ with $\alpha, C$ depending only on $n$.

proofs.name: Potential estimate and series
proofs.slogan: Bound $u$ by a Riesz potential of $|\nabla u|$, estimate its $L^q$ norms with $q^{1-1/n}$ growth, and sum the exponential series.
proofs.scope: The inequality with some constant $\alpha$; Moser's sharp constant $\alpha_n$ is not proved. Below, $n' = n/(n-1)$ and $\omega_n$ is the volume of the unit ball.

roles.why: Boundedness gives $|\Omega| < \infty$, which enters every $L^q$ estimate through the factor $|\Omega|^{1/q}$.
The $W_0^{1,n}$ condition allows approximation by smooth compactly supported functions, and the bound $\|\nabla u\|_n \le 1$ normalizes the estimates.

steps.slogan: Reduce to smooth compactly supported functions by density and Fatou's lemma.
steps.detail: The space $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ is dense in $W_0^{1,n}(\Omega)$, so choose $u_j \in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $u_j \to u$ almost everywhere and in $W^{1,n}$, rescaled so that $\|\nabla u_j\|_n \le 1$. Fatou's lemma passes the integral estimate from the $u_j$ to $u$.

steps.slogan: Bound $|u(x)|$ by a Riesz potential of $|\nabla u|$.
steps.detail: For $u \in C_c^1(\Omega)$ write $u(x) = -\int_0^\infty \partial_r u(x + r\theta)\,dr$ for each unit vector $\theta$, and average over the sphere. This gives $|u(x)| \le \frac{1}{n\omega_n}\int_\Omega \frac{|\nabla u(y)|}{|x-y|^{n-1}}\,dy$.

steps.slogan: Bound the $L^q$ norms of the potential by $c_n q^{1-1/n}|\Omega|^{1/q}$ with Young's inequality for kernels.
steps.detail: Fix $q \ge n$ and set $1/r = 1 - 1/n + 1/q$. Young's inequality for the integral operator with kernel $|x-y|^{1-n}$ on $\Omega$ bounds $\|u\|_q$ by $\|\nabla u\|_n$ times the $L^r$ norm of the kernel on a ball of volume $|\Omega|$. The radial integral shows that this norm is at most $c_n q^{1-1/n}|\Omega|^{1/q}$, with $c_n$ independent of $q$.

steps.slogan: Expand the exponential and bound the $k$-th term by $(\alpha c)^k|\Omega|$ for large $k$.
steps.detail: We have $\int_\Omega e^{\alpha|u|^{n'}} = \sum_k \frac{\alpha^k}{k!}\int_\Omega |u|^{kn'}$. For $kn' \ge n$, step 3 with $q = kn'$ gives $\int |u|^{kn'} \le (c_n^{n'} n')^k k^k|\Omega|$, and $k^k \le e^k k!$. The finitely many terms with $kn' < n$ are at most $c\,|\Omega|$ by Hölder's inequality and step 3 with $q = n$.

steps.slogan: Choose $\alpha$ small so that the series is dominated by a [geometric series](c:geometric-series).
steps.detail: Take $\alpha$ with $\alpha\, c_n^{n'} n' e \le 1/2$. Then the terms with $kn' \ge n$ add up to at most $2|\Omega|$, and the finitely many other terms add up to at most $c\,|\Omega|$. With step 1, this gives $\int_\Omega e^{\alpha|u|^{n'}} \le C|\Omega|$ for every admissible $u$.

concepts.c:sobolev-space: The functions $u$ come from $W_0^{1,n}$, which the smooth functions approximate.
concepts.c:orlicz-space: The estimate says that $W_0^{1,n}$ embeds into an exponential Orlicz space.
concepts.c:geometric-series: A geometric majorant sums the exponential series with a uniform constant.

source.note: Trudinger's argument as in Gilbarg and Trudinger, Elliptic Partial Differential Equations of Second Order, Section 7.8 (Theorem 7.15).

statement: Every [inverse semigroup](c:inverse-semigroup) $S$ embeds in the symmetric inverse monoid $I(S)$ of [partial bijections](c:partial-bijection) of the set $S$: there is an injective [homomorphism](c:homomorphism) $\rho\colon S \to I(S)$ with $\rho(s^{-1}) = \rho(s)^{-1}$.

hypotheses.text: The semigroup $S$ is an [inverse semigroup](c:inverse-semigroup): each $s$ has a unique $s^{-1}$ with $ss^{-1}s = s$ and $s^{-1}ss^{-1} = s^{-1}$.

conclusion: There is an injective homomorphism $\rho\colon S \to I(S)$ of semigroups with $\rho(s^{-1}) = \rho(s)^{-1}$ for all $s$.

proofs.name: Partial left translations
proofs.slogan: Let each element act by left multiplication, restricted to the set where it is injective, and check that this is an injective homomorphism.
proofs.scope: All inverse semigroups, including the empty and the one-element case. For a group every $\rho_s$ is total, and the proof gives Cayley's theorem.

roles.why: Unique inverses give the commuting [idempotents](c:idempotent) and the rules for inverses that every step uses.

steps.slogan: Collect the structure facts about idempotents and inverses in an inverse semigroup.
steps.detail: In an [inverse semigroup](c:inverse-semigroup), $ss^{-1}$ and $s^{-1}s$ are [idempotents](c:idempotent), any two idempotents commute, $(s^{-1})^{-1} = s$ and $(st)^{-1} = t^{-1}s^{-1}$. These standard facts (Vagner) are the only input from the hypothesis.

steps.slogan: Define $\rho_s$ as left multiplication by $s$ on the set $D_s = s^{-1}S$.
steps.detail: We have $D_s = \{x : s^{-1}sx = x\}$ and $\rho_s(x) = sx \in sS$. For $x \in D_s$, $s^{-1}(sx) = x$, and for $y = sz \in sS$, $s(s^{-1}y) = ss^{-1}sz = y$. So $\rho_s\colon D_s \to sS$ is a [partial bijection](c:partial-bijection) with inverse $\rho_{s^{-1}}$, which gives $\rho(s^{-1}) = \rho(s)^{-1}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\rho_s\rho_t = \rho_{st}$ by comparing domains and values.
steps.detail: The domain of $\rho_s\rho_t$ is $\{x \in D_t : tx \in D_s\}$. If $x = t^{-1}s^{-1}z \in D_{st}$, then $tx = tt^{-1}s^{-1}z \in D_s$ because idempotents commute; conversely, if $x \in D_t$ and $tx \in D_s$, then $x = t^{-1}s^{-1}s(tx) \in D_{st}$. On this domain $s(tx) = (st)x$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\rho_s = \rho_t$ forces $s = t$ by evaluating at an idempotent.
steps.detail: If $\rho_s = \rho_t$, then $D_s = D_t$. The idempotent $e = s^{-1}s$ lies in $D_s = D_t$, so $t^{-1}te = e$, and $t^{-1}t \in D_s$ gives $s^{-1}s\,t^{-1}t = t^{-1}t$; idempotents commute, so $e = t^{-1}t$. Then $s = se = \rho_s(e) = \rho_t(e) = te = t$.

steps.slogan: Combine the steps: $\rho$ is an injective homomorphism that respects inverses.
steps.detail: Step 3 shows that $\rho$ is a homomorphism into $I(S)$, step 4 that it is injective, and step 2 that $\rho(s^{-1}) = \rho(s)^{-1}$. So $\rho$ embeds $S$ into $I(S)$.

concepts.c:inverse-semigroup: Unique inverses are what make left translations partial bijections.
concepts.c:partial-bijection: Each element acts as a partial bijection of the set $S$.
concepts.c:idempotent: Commuting idempotents control the domains of the partial maps.
concepts.c:homomorphism: The map $\rho$ must respect the product, which step 3 checks.

source.note: The Vagner-Preston representation by partial left translations; see Howie, Fundamentals of Semigroup Theory, Chapter 5.

statement: Let $C$ be a smooth projective [algebraic curve](c:algebraic-curve) over an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field) $K$, and let $f, g$ be nonzero [rational functions](c:rational-function) on $C$ with [divisors](c:divisor) of disjoint support. Then $\prod_P f(P)^{\operatorname{ord}_P g} = \prod_P g(P)^{\operatorname{ord}_P f}$.

hypotheses.text: The curve $C$ is a smooth projective [algebraic curve](c:algebraic-curve) over an algebraically closed field $K$.
The functions $f, g \in K(C)^\times$ have [divisors](c:divisor) with disjoint supports.

conclusion: The two finite products $\prod_P f(P)^{\operatorname{ord}_P g}$ and $\prod_P g(P)^{\operatorname{ord}_P f}$ are equal.

proofs.name: Norm to the projective line
proofs.slogan: Read both sides along the finite map $g\colon C \to \mathbb{P}^1$, replace $f$ by its norm in $K(t)$, and compute on the projective line.
proofs.scope: A nonconstant $g$; for constant $g = c$ both sides equal $1$ because $\operatorname{ord}_P g = 0$ and $\deg \operatorname{div} f = 0$. Both products are finite since only finitely many orders are nonzero.

roles.why: Smoothness and properness make $g$ a finite map to the projective line and give orders of vanishing at every point.
Disjoint divisors make $f$ a unit over $0$ and $\infty$, so both products are defined and the norm formulas apply.

steps.slogan: Read the left side as a ratio of values of $f$ on the fibres of $g$ over $0$ and $\infty$.
steps.detail: The nonconstant $g$ is a finite map $C \to \mathbb{P}^1$. The order $\operatorname{ord}_P g$ is $e_P$ over $0$, is $-e_P$ over $\infty$, and is $0$ elsewhere, with $e_P$ the ramification index. So the left side is $\prod_{P \mapsto 0} f(P)^{e_P} \big/ \prod_{P \mapsto \infty} f(P)^{e_P}$, and $f$ is a unit at all these points.

steps.slogan: Replace $f$ by its norm $N(f) \in K(t)$ along the [field extension](c:field-extension) $K(C)/K(t)$ with $t = g$.
steps.detail: The [function field](c:function-field) $K(C)$ is a finite extension of $K(t)$. At a point $a$ over which $f$ is a unit, $N(f)(a) = \prod_{P \mapsto a} f(P)^{e_P}$, the determinant of multiplication by $f$ on the fibre algebra $\prod_P K[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^{e_P})$, and $\operatorname{ord}_a N(f) = \sum_{P \mapsto a}\operatorname{ord}_P f$ since all residue fields equal $K$. So the left side is $N(f)(0)/N(f)(\infty)$.

steps.slogan: Compute $N(f)(0)/N(f)(\infty)$ on the [projective line](c:projective-line) from the factorization of $N(f)$.
steps.detail: Write $N(f) = c\prod_i (t-a_i)^{n_i}$. Because $f$ has no zero or pole over $0$ or $\infty$, every $a_i \ne 0$ and $\sum n_i = 0$. Then $N(f)(0) = c\prod(-a_i)^{n_i} = c\prod a_i^{n_i}$ and $N(f)(\infty) = c$, so the left side equals $\prod_i a_i^{n_i}$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the right side with the same norm formula for orders.
steps.detail: Since $g(P) = t(P)$, the right side is $\prod_a a^{\sum_{P \mapsto a}\operatorname{ord}_P f}$ over $a \in K^\times$, because $\operatorname{ord}_P f = 0$ over $0$ and $\infty$. By the order formula of step 2 this is $\prod_a a^{\operatorname{ord}_a N(f)} = \prod_i a_i^{n_i}$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two evaluations to obtain the reciprocity law.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give the same value $\prod_i a_i^{n_i}$ for the two products. So $\prod_P f(P)^{\operatorname{ord}_P g} = \prod_P g(P)^{\operatorname{ord}_P f}$.

concepts.c:algebraic-curve: The theorem is about functions on a smooth projective curve.
concepts.c:algebraically-closed-field: Algebraic closure makes all residue fields equal $K$.
concepts.c:rational-function: The functions $f$ and $g$ are rational functions on the curve.
concepts.c:divisor: Disjoint divisors keep $f$ a unit where $g$ vanishes or has a pole.
concepts.c:field-extension: The norm is taken along the finite extension $K(C)/K(t)$.
concepts.c:function-field: The function field $K(C)$ carries the norm to $K(t)$.
concepts.c:projective-line: On the projective line every rational function factors into linear terms.

source.note: The norm argument that reduces Weil reciprocity to the projective line; see Serre, Groupes algébriques et corps de classes, Chapter III.

statement: Let $F, G$ be [functors](c:functor) from a category with models $\mathcal{M}$ to nonnegative [chain complexes](c:chain-complex), with $F$ free on models and $G$ acyclic on models. Then each natural map $H_0F \to H_0G$ is induced by a natural chain map $F \to G$, unique up to natural chain homotopy.

hypotheses.text: Each $F_n$ is free on models: there are models $M_i$ and elements $b_i \in F_n(M_i)$ such that the elements $F_n(f)(b_i)$, over all morphisms $f\colon M_i \to X$, form a [basis](c:basis) of $F_n(X)$ for every object $X$.
For each model $M$ and each $k \ge 1$, the [homology](c:homology) group $H_k(G(M))$ is zero.
The map $\varphi\colon H_0F \to H_0G$ is a [natural transformation](c:natural-transformation).

conclusion: There is a natural [chain map](c:chain-map) $\Phi\colon F \to G$ that induces $\varphi$ on $H_0$, and any two such maps are naturally [chain homotopic](c:chain-homotopy).

proofs.name: Induction on the degree
proofs.slogan: Choose images of the basis elements degree by degree, solving each boundary equation in the acyclic complex of a model.
proofs.scope: Existence and uniqueness up to homotopy. The corollary that two homology theories agree on a category of spaces is not proved here.

roles.why: Freeness lets one define natural maps by choosing images of the basis elements only.
Acyclicity of $G(M)$ turns cycles of positive degree into boundaries, which solves each lifting problem.
Naturality of $\varphi$ makes the degree-zero lift induce $\varphi$ and kills the obstruction in degree one.

steps.slogan: Define a natural map on a free functor by choosing images of the [basis](c:basis) elements.
steps.detail: The elements $F_n(f)(b_i)$ form a basis of $F_n(X)$. So choosing any $\Phi(b_i) \in G_n(M_i)$ and setting $\Phi(F_n(f)b_i) = G_n(f)\Phi(b_i)$ defines a natural transformation $F_n \to G_n$. Naturality holds on basis elements because $F_n(h)F_n(f)b_i = F_n(hf)b_i$, and so on all of $F_n(X)$.

steps.slogan: Lift $\varphi$ to degree zero by choosing representatives of $\varphi[b_i]$.
steps.detail: For a basis element $b_i \in F_0(M_i)$, the class $\varphi[b_i] \in H_0G(M_i) = G_0(M_i)/\partial G_1(M_i)$ has a representative $g_i$. Set $\Phi_0(b_i) = g_i$ and extend by step 1. Naturality of $\varphi$ shows $[\Phi_0 x] = \varphi[x]$ on every basis element, hence on all of $F_0(X)$.

steps.slogan: Build $\Phi_n$ inductively by solving $\partial g = \Phi_{n-1}\partial b$ in $G_n(M)$.
steps.detail: For a basis element $b \in F_n(M)$ let $z = \Phi_{n-1}\partial b$. For $n = 1$, $[z] = \varphi[\partial b] = 0$ in $H_0$, so $z$ is a boundary. For $n \ge 2$, $\partial z = \Phi_{n-2}\partial\partial b = 0$, so $z$ is a cycle of positive degree and a boundary by acyclicity. Pick $g$ with $\partial g = z$, set $\Phi_n(b) = g$ and extend by step 1.

steps.slogan: Build a natural chain homotopy between two lifts by the same inductive method.
steps.detail: Let $\Phi, \Psi$ both induce $\varphi$. We build natural $s_n\colon F_n \to G_{n+1}$ with $\partial s_n + s_{n-1}\partial = \Phi_n - \Psi_n$. For a basis element $b$, the element $z = \Phi_n b - \Psi_n b - s_{n-1}\partial b$ is a cycle for $n \ge 1$ and has class $0$ in $H_0$ for $n = 0$, so $z = \partial g$ for some $g$ (by acyclicity if $n \ge 1$); set $s_n(b) = g$ and extend by step 1.

steps.slogan: Collect existence and uniqueness into the statement of the theorem.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give a natural chain map $\Phi$ that induces $\varphi$ on $H_0$. Step 4 shows that any two such maps differ by a natural chain homotopy.

concepts.c:functor: The theorem concerns natural constructions on all objects at once.
concepts.c:chain-complex: The functors take values in nonnegative chain complexes.
concepts.c:homology: Acyclicity on models is vanishing of positive-degree homology.
concepts.c:natural-transformation: The given map $\varphi$ and the constructed $\Phi$ are natural.
concepts.c:chain-map: The constructed $\Phi$ commutes with the boundary maps.
concepts.c:chain-homotopy: Two lifts are shown to be naturally chain homotopic.
concepts.c:basis: The basis lets one define $\Phi$ by free choices of images.

source.note: The inductive construction of Eilenberg and Mac Lane, Acyclic models, Amer. J. Math. 75 (1953).

statement: Let $F, G, H \in \mathbb{C}[x,y,z]$ be forms that define plane [algebraic curves](c:algebraic-curve), with $F$ and $G$ having no common component. If, at every point $P$ of $V(F) \cap V(G)$, $H$ lies in the ideal $(F,G)$ of the [local ring](c:local-ring) $\mathcal{O}_P$, then $H = AF + BG$ for forms $A, B$.

hypotheses.text: The forms $F, G$ define [algebraic curves](c:algebraic-curve) in $\mathbb{P}^2$ without a common component.
At every point $P \in V(F) \cap V(G)$ the form $H$ lies in $(F,G)$ in the [local ring](c:local-ring) $\mathcal{O}_P$ of the plane at $P$.

conclusion: There are homogeneous polynomials $A, B$, of degrees $\deg H - \deg F$ and $\deg H - \deg G$, with $H = AF + BG$.

proofs.name: Unmixedness of a complete intersection
proofs.slogan: Show that $(F,G)$ is a complete intersection without embedded components, so membership in $(F,G)$ can be tested at each intersection point.
proofs.scope: Complex projective plane; the same proof works over any algebraically closed field. The local hypothesis is not vacuous, because two plane curves always meet.

roles.why: Coprime forms give a regular sequence, so $(F,G)$ is unmixed with finitely many isolated points.
Membership of $H$ in each primary component is exactly the local condition at the corresponding point.

steps.slogan: Show that $F, G$ form a [regular sequence](c:regular-sequence) in $S = \mathbb{C}[x,y,z]$.
steps.detail: The ring $S$ is a [unique factorization domain](c:unique-factorization-domain), and $F \ne 0$ is a nonzerodivisor. If $Gh \in (F)$, then $F \mid Gh$, and since $F, G$ are coprime, $F \mid h$. So $G$ is a nonzerodivisor modulo $F$.

steps.slogan: Deduce that $(F,G)$ has no embedded primes and no irrelevant component.
steps.detail: The quotient $S/(F,G)$ is a complete intersection of dimension $1$, hence a [Cohen-Macaulay ring](c:cohen-macaulay-ring). Macaulay's unmixedness theorem says that it has no embedded [associated primes](c:associated-prime). So every associated prime of $(F,G)$ is minimal of height $2$, and the irrelevant ideal $(x,y,z)$ of height $3$ is not associated.

steps.slogan: Identify the associated primes with the points of $V(F) \cap V(G)$.
steps.detail: Since $F, G$ are coprime, $V(F) \cap V(G)$ is a finite set of points of $\mathbb{P}^2$. The homogeneous primes of height $2$ that contain $(F,G)$ are exactly the ideals $\mathfrak{p}_P$ of these points $P$.

steps.slogan: Write $(F,G)$ as the intersection of its local primary components.
steps.detail: By [primary decomposition](c:primary-ideal), $(F,G) = \bigcap_P Q_P$ with $Q_P$ a $\mathfrak{p}_P$-primary ideal, and no component is embedded by step 2. Each $Q_P$ is isolated, so $Q_P = (F,G)S_{\mathfrak{p}_P} \cap S$. Hence $H \in (F,G)$ if and only if $H \in (F,G)S_{\mathfrak{p}_P}$ for every $P$.

steps.slogan: Match membership in $S_{\mathfrak{p}_P}$ with membership in $\mathcal{O}_P$ and conclude.
steps.detail: Choose a linear form $L$ with $L(P) \ne 0$. Then $S[1/L] = \mathbb{C}[u,v][L,L^{-1}]$ with $u = x/L$, $v = y/L$, so $H \in (F,G)S_{\mathfrak{p}_P}$ is the hypothesis in $\mathcal{O}_P$ for the dehomogenizations. By step 4, $H = AF + BG$ with $A, B \in S$; taking the components of degrees $\deg H - \deg F$ and $\deg H - \deg G$ makes them homogeneous.

concepts.c:algebraic-curve: The forms $F$ and $G$ define the two curves that meet in finitely many points.
concepts.c:local-ring: The hypothesis is membership in $(F,G)$ in the local ring at each point.
concepts.c:regular-sequence: A regular sequence makes $S/(F,G)$ a complete intersection.
concepts.c:unique-factorization-domain: Unique factorization turns coprimality of $F, G$ into regularity.
concepts.c:cohen-macaulay-ring: Cohen-Macaulayness rules out embedded components of $(F,G)$.
concepts.c:associated-prime: Associated primes of $(F,G)$ are shown to be the points of the intersection.
concepts.c:primary-ideal: The ideal $(F,G)$ is the intersection of primary components, one per point.

source.note: Max Noether's fundamental theorem via unmixedness of complete intersections; see Fulton, Algebraic Curves, Chapter 5, for the classical treatment.

statement: Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a nonempty [family of sets](c:family-of-sets) of subsets of an $n$-element set $X$, $n \ge 1$, with $\emptyset \notin \mathcal{A}$. For $A \subseteq X$ let $I(A)$ be the intersection of all $B \in \mathcal{A}$ with $B \subseteq A$, and $\emptyset$ if there is none. Then $\sum_{\emptyset \ne A \subseteq X} \frac{|I(A)|}{|A|\binom{n}{|A|}} = 1$.

hypotheses.text: The ground set $X$ is a [finite set](c:finite-set) with $n \ge 1$ elements.
The family $\mathcal{A}$ is nonempty.
The empty set is not a member of $\mathcal{A}$.

conclusion: The weighted sum of the sizes $|I(A)|$ over the nonempty subsets $A \subseteq X$ equals $1$.

formal.difference: The declaration sums over all subsets of a finite nonempty type and reads division by zero as $0$. The term for $A = \emptyset$ is then $0$, as in this statement.

proofs.name: Complement duality and telescoping
proofs.slogan: Pair the sum with a dual sum of truncated suprema, compute the dual sum by induction with a telescoping base case, and complement twice.
proofs.scope: All nonempty families avoiding $\emptyset$; the sums over $A$ read terms with zero denominator as $0$. Write $H_n = \sum_{k=1}^n 1/k$.

roles.why: Finiteness and $n \ge 1$ make all sums finite and give the harmonic total $nH_n$.
Nonemptiness starts the induction and makes the complement family nonempty.
Since $\emptyset \notin \mathcal{A}$, the complement family does not contain $X$, which the dual formula needs.

steps.slogan: Define the truncated infimum and supremum of $\mathcal{A}$ and the two weighted sums.
steps.detail: Let $I_{\mathcal{A}}(A)$ be as in the statement and $U_{\mathcal{A}}(A) = \bigcup\{B \in \mathcal{A} : A \subseteq B\}$, or $X$ if there is no such $B$. Put $\mathrm{inf}(\mathcal{A}) = \sum_A \frac{|I_{\mathcal{A}}(A)|}{|A|\binom{n}{|A|}}$ and $\mathrm{sup}(\mathcal{A}) = \sum_A \frac{|U_{\mathcal{A}}(A)|}{(n-|A|)\binom{n}{|A|}}$; the claim is $\mathrm{inf}(\mathcal{A}) = 1$, and terms with zero denominator are $0$.

steps.slogan: Reflect by complements to relate $\mathrm{inf}(\mathcal{A}^c)$ and $\mathrm{sup}(\mathcal{A})$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal{A}^c = \{X \setminus B\}$. Then $X \setminus U_{\mathcal{A}}(A) = I_{\mathcal{A}^c}(X \setminus A)$, so $|I_{\mathcal{A}^c}(X\setminus A)| + |U_{\mathcal{A}}(A)| = n$. Reindex by $A \mapsto X \setminus A$, with $\binom{n}{n-j} = \binom{n}{j}$, and group by $|A| = j$: $\mathrm{inf}(\mathcal{A}^c) + \mathrm{sup}(\mathcal{A}) = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \frac{n}{n-j} = nH_n$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\mathrm{sup}(\{B\}) = nH_n - 1$ for one proper subset $B$ by telescoping.
steps.detail: For $B \ne X$, $U_{\{B\}}(A) = B$ if $A \subseteq B$ and $X$ otherwise, so $\mathrm{sup}(\{B\}) = nH_n - \sum_{i=0}^{b}\binom{b}{i}\frac{n-b}{(n-i)\binom{n}{i}}$ with $b = |B|$. With $f(i) = \binom{b}{i}/\binom{n}{i}$, the $i$-th term equals $f(i) - f(i+1)$, so the sum telescopes to $f(0) - f(b+1) = 1$.

steps.slogan: Prove $\mathrm{sup}(\mathcal{B}) = nH_n - 1$ for every nonempty $\mathcal{B}$ with $X \notin \mathcal{B}$ by strong induction.
steps.detail: For $\mathcal{B} = \{B\} \cup \mathcal{B}'$ use the termwise identity $\mathrm{sup}(\mathcal{C} \cup \mathcal{D}) + \mathrm{sup}(\mathcal{C} \sqcap \mathcal{D}) = \mathrm{sup}(\mathcal{C}) + \mathrm{sup}(\mathcal{D})$, where $\mathcal{C} \sqcap \mathcal{D} = \{C \cap D\}$. The families $\mathcal{B}'$ and $\{B\} \sqcap \mathcal{B}'$ are nonempty, smaller, and avoid $X$. By step 3 and induction all three other terms equal $nH_n - 1$, so $\mathrm{sup}(\mathcal{B}) = nH_n - 1$.

steps.slogan: Complement $\mathcal{A}$ and read $\mathrm{inf}(\mathcal{A}) = nH_n - (nH_n - 1) = 1$.
steps.detail: Since $\emptyset \notin \mathcal{A}$, the family $\mathcal{A}^c$ is nonempty and does not contain $X$. Step 4 gives $\mathrm{sup}(\mathcal{A}^c) = nH_n - 1$. Step 2 for the family $\mathcal{A}^c$, whose complement family is $\mathcal{A}$, gives $\mathrm{inf}(\mathcal{A}) = nH_n - \mathrm{sup}(\mathcal{A}^c) = 1$.

concepts.c:family-of-sets: The identity concerns a family of subsets and its truncated intersections.
concepts.c:finite-set: Finiteness of the ground set makes all sums finite.

source.note: mathlib uses infSum_compls_add_supSum (complement duality), supSum_singleton with binomial_sum_eq (telescoping), supSum_union_add_supSum_infs with strong induction in supSum_of_univ_notMem, then complements twice.

statement: Let $G$ be a connected [reductive group](c:reductive-group) over $\mathbb{Q}$ and $f \in C_c^\infty(G(\mathbb{A})^1)$. Then $\sum_{\mathfrak{o}} J_{\mathfrak{o}}(f) = \sum_{\chi} J_\chi(f)$. The geometric terms $J_{\mathfrak{o}}$ are weighted orbital integrals over classes $\mathfrak{o}$, and the spectral terms $J_\chi$ come from [automorphic forms](c:automorphic-form) and Eisenstein series.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a connected [reductive group](c:reductive-group) over $\mathbb{Q}$.
The function $f$ is smooth with compact support on $G(\mathbb{A})^1$.

conclusion: The geometric and the spectral expansion of Arthur's truncated kernel integral give the same value: $\sum_{\mathfrak{o}} J_{\mathfrak{o}}(f) = \sum_\chi J_\chi(f)$.

proofs.name: Truncated kernel
proofs.slogan: Truncate the kernel of $R(f)$ near the cusps, expand its integral over conjugacy classes and over cuspidal data, and equate the two expansions.
proofs.scope: An outline of Arthur's coarse (non-invariant) trace formula; the cited papers give each step in full. The invariant and stable trace formulas are other members of the family.

roles.why: Reductivity gives the parabolic subgroups, Levi components and Eisenstein series that truncation and the spectral side use.
Smoothness and compact support make the kernel of $R(f)$ well behaved and give absolute convergence of both expansions.

steps.slogan: Write $R(f)$ as an integral operator with the kernel $K(x,y) = \sum_{\gamma \in G(\mathbb{Q})} f(x^{-1}\gamma y)$.
steps.detail: The operator $R(f)$ acts on $L^2(G(\mathbb{Q}) \backslash G(\mathbb{A})^1)$ by right translation. This is the start of Selberg's trace formula. For a noncompact quotient the integral $\int K(x,x)\,dx$ diverges, so $R(f)$ is not of trace class.

steps.slogan: Truncate the kernel with Arthur's operator $\Lambda^T$ so that its diagonal integral converges.
steps.detail: Arthur's truncation operator removes the growth of the kernel near the cusps, using the parabolic subgroups of $G$. The integral $J^T(f)$ of the truncated kernel over the diagonal converges absolutely and is a polynomial function of the truncation parameter $T$.

steps.slogan: Expand $J^T(f)$ over classes of $G(\mathbb{Q})$ into weighted orbital integrals.
steps.detail: Group the terms of the kernel by [conjugacy classes](c:conjugacy-class) $\mathfrak{o}$ of $G(\mathbb{Q})$, taken by semisimple part. Arthur proves that each $J_{\mathfrak{o}}^T(f)$ converges and that $\sum_{\mathfrak{o}} J_{\mathfrak{o}}^T(f)$ converges absolutely. The terms are weighted orbital integrals.

steps.slogan: Expand $J^T(f)$ spectrally with Langlands' theory of [Eisenstein series](c:eisenstein-series).
steps.detail: Langlands' spectral decomposition of $L^2(G(\mathbb{Q}) \backslash G(\mathbb{A})^1)$ expresses the kernel through cuspidal data $\chi$ and residues of Eisenstein series. Applying the same truncation to this expression gives $J^T(f) = \sum_\chi J_\chi^T(f)$, again absolutely convergent.

steps.slogan: Equate the two expansions of $J^T(f)$ and evaluate at a base point.
steps.detail: Both expansions equal the same function $J^T(f)$ of $T$, so they agree as polynomials in $T$. Their common value at a fixed base point $T_0$ gives $\sum_{\mathfrak{o}} J_{\mathfrak{o}}(f) = \sum_\chi J_\chi(f)$.

concepts.c:reductive-group: Its parabolic subgroups define the truncation and the Eisenstein series.
concepts.c:automorphic-form: The spectral terms are built from automorphic forms on $G$.
concepts.c:conjugacy-class: Geometric terms are indexed by classes of rational elements.
concepts.c:eisenstein-series: Eisenstein series describe the continuous part of the spectral expansion.

source.ref: J. Arthur, A trace formula for reductive groups I: terms associated to classes in G(Q), Duke Mathematical Journal 45 (1978), 911-952; II: applications of a truncation operator, Compositio Mathematica 40 (1980), 87-121
source.note: The first paper treats the geometric expansion of the truncated kernel and the second applies the truncation operator to the spectral side; see also Arthur's introduction to the trace formula, Clay Mathematics Proceedings 4 (2005).

statement: Let $K$ be an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field), $V \subseteq K^n$ the [zero locus](c:zero-locus) of an ideal of $K[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, and $P\colon K^n \to K^n$ a polynomial map with $P(V) \subseteq V$ that is injective on $V$. Then $P(V) = V$.

hypotheses.text: The field $K$ is [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field).
The set $V \subseteq K^n$ is the [zero locus](c:zero-locus) of an ideal $I \subseteq K[x_1,\dots,x_n]$.
The map $P = (p_1,\dots,p_n)$ has polynomial components, satisfies $P(V) \subseteq V$ and is injective on $V$.

conclusion: The map $P$ sends $V$ onto $V$, so it is surjective on $V$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the same implication, with $V$ given by an ideal and the coordinates indexed by a finite type. The bijectivity of injective polynomial self-maps of $K^n$ is the case $I = 0$ (ax_grothendieck_univ).

proofs.name: Finite fields and the Lefschetz principle
proofs.slogan: Prove the claim for algebraic extensions of finite fields by a finiteness argument, then transfer it to all algebraically closed fields by completeness and compactness.
proofs.scope: Every characteristic and every $n$; for $K = \mathbb{C}$ and $V = \mathbb{C}^n$, every injective polynomial self-map of $\mathbb{C}^n$ is bijective. The base case uses only that an injective self-map of a finite set is onto.

roles.why: Completeness of the theory of algebraically closed fields of a given characteristic transfers the finite-field case to $K$.
A finitely generated ideal makes $V$ definable by one first-order formula, so the claim is a first-order sentence.
The two properties $P(V) \subseteq V$ and injectivity on $V$ are the premises of the sentence, and the finite case restricts $P$ to a finite subring.

steps.slogan: Express the claim as one sentence of [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic) about polynomial maps of bounded degree.
steps.detail: By Hilbert's basis theorem $I = (q_1,\dots,q_r)$, so $V$ is defined by a formula $\varphi$ with the coefficients of the $q_j$ as parameters. For fixed $n$, $r$ and degree bound $d$, the statement ``for all parameters and all $P$ of degree at most $d$, if $P$ maps $V$ into $V$ and is injective on $V$, then it is onto $V$'' is one sentence $\sigma$.

steps.slogan: Prove the claim for algebraic extensions of a [finite field](c:finite-field) by restricting $P$ to a finite subring.
steps.detail: Let $R$ be an [algebraic extension](c:algebraic-extension) of a finite field $k$, and let $S \subseteq R^n$ satisfy $P(S) \subseteq S$ with $P$ injective on $S$. For a target $v \in S$, let $R_0$ be the finite $k$-algebra generated by the coefficients of $P$ and the coordinates of $v$. Then $S \cap R_0^n$ is finite and $P$ maps it injectively into itself, hence onto itself, so $v$ has a preimage.

steps.slogan: Transfer the sentence to every algebraically closed field of prime characteristic $p$.
steps.detail: The algebraic closure of $\mathbb{F}_p$ is algebraic over $\mathbb{F}_p$, so it satisfies $\sigma$ by step 2. The theory of algebraically closed fields of characteristic $p$ is a [complete theory](c:complete-theory), so every such field satisfies $\sigma$.

steps.slogan: Transfer the sentence to characteristic $0$ by the Lefschetz principle.
steps.detail: A sentence holds in the algebraically closed fields of characteristic $0$ if and only if it holds in those of infinitely many prime characteristics, by the compactness theorem. By step 3, $\sigma$ holds in all prime characteristics, so it holds in characteristic $0$.

steps.slogan: Instantiate the sentence of the right characteristic at the data of $V$ and $P$.
steps.detail: The characteristic of $K$ is $0$ or prime, so $K$ satisfies $\sigma$ by step 4 or step 3. Apply $\sigma$ to the parameters of $V$ and the coefficients of $P$. The premises $P(V) \subseteq V$ and injectivity on $V$ hold, so $P$ maps $V$ onto $V$.

concepts.c:algebraically-closed-field: Completeness of its theory lets one test the claim in one convenient field.
concepts.c:zero-locus: The set $V$ is the zero locus, defined by finitely many polynomial equations.
concepts.c:first-order-logic: The claim is turned into one sentence that transfers between fields.
concepts.c:finite-field: Injective self-maps of finite sets are onto, which settles the base case.
concepts.c:algebraic-extension: Algebraic extensions of finite fields are locally finite.
concepts.c:complete-theory: Completeness gives the sentence in all fields of one characteristic.

statement: Let $K$ and $L$ be [compact Hausdorff spaces](c:compact-hausdorff-space). The spaces $C(K)$ and $C(L)$ of real [continuous functions](c:c-k-space) with the sup norm are isometrically isomorphic if and only if $K$ and $L$ are [homeomorphic](c:homeomorphism).

hypotheses.text: The spaces $K$ and $L$ are [compact Hausdorff spaces](c:compact-hausdorff-space).

conclusion: The spaces $C(K)$ and $C(L)$ are isometrically isomorphic if and only if $K$ and $L$ are homeomorphic.

proofs.name: Extreme points of the dual ball
proofs.slogan: A surjective isometry has an adjoint that maps the extreme points of the dual ball, the point masses, to point masses, and this gives a homeomorphism.
proofs.scope: Real scalars and surjective linear isometries. In the complex case the extreme points are $\lambda\delta_k$ with $|\lambda| = 1$, and the same proof works with a unimodular function $h$.

roles.why: Compactness gives the Riesz representation by measures, and the Hausdorff property with Urysohn's lemma makes the points of $K$ and $L$ recoverable from functions.

steps.slogan: Turn a homeomorphism into a surjective isometry by composition.
steps.detail: If $\varphi\colon L \to K$ is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism), then $Tf = f \circ \varphi$ is linear and bijective with inverse $g \mapsto g \circ \varphi^{-1}$. It preserves the sup norm because $\varphi$ is onto. This proves the direction ``if''.

steps.slogan: Identify the extreme points of the unit ball of the dual of $C(K)$ as the measures $\pm\delta_k$.
steps.detail: By the Riesz-Markov-Kakutani theorem, the dual of $C(K)$ is the space of signed Radon measures with the total variation norm. If $|\mu|$ has two points in its support, an open $U$ that separates them gives $\mu = \mu|_U + \mu|_{U^c}$, a nontrivial convex combination of norm one measures, so $\mu$ is not extreme. Thus an [extreme point](c:extreme-point) is a [Dirac measure](c:dirac-measure) $\pm\delta_k$, and each $\pm\delta_k$ is extreme.

steps.slogan: Map point masses by the adjoint of $T$ to get $\varphi\colon L \to K$ and signs $h(l)$.
steps.detail: Let $T\colon C(K) \to C(L)$ be a surjective [linear isometry](c:linear-isometry). Its adjoint is an affine bijection of the dual balls, so it maps extreme points to extreme points: $T^*\delta_l = h(l)\,\delta_{\varphi(l)}$ with $h(l) = \pm1$. Hence $(Tf)(l) = h(l) f(\varphi(l))$, and $f = 1$ gives $h = T1$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\varphi$ is continuous because $f \circ \varphi = h \cdot Tf$ for every $f$.
steps.detail: The function $h = T1$ is continuous and $h^2 = 1$, so $f \circ \varphi = h \cdot Tf$ is continuous on $L$ for every $f \in C(K)$. The topology of the compact Hausdorff space $K$ is the weakest one that makes every $f \in C(K)$ continuous, by Urysohn's lemma. So $\varphi$ is continuous.

steps.slogan: Show that $\varphi$ is bijective, hence a homeomorphism, because $T$ is onto.
steps.detail: If $\varphi(l_1) = \varphi(l_2)$, then $h(l_1)(Tf)(l_1) = h(l_2)(Tf)(l_2)$ for all $f$; since $T$ is onto, this holds for every $g \in C(L)$, so $l_1 = l_2$ by Urysohn's lemma. If $k \notin \varphi(L)$, some $f \in C(K)$ with $f(k) = 1$ vanishes on the compact set $\varphi(L)$, so $Tf = 0$ and $f = 0$, which is false. A continuous bijection from a compact space onto a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism.

steps.slogan: Combine the two directions to get the equivalence.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives an isometric isomorphism from a homeomorphism. Steps 2 to 5 give a homeomorphism from an isometric isomorphism. Together they prove the equivalence.

concepts.c:compact-hausdorff-space: Compact Hausdorff spaces are the ones recovered from their function spaces.
concepts.c:c-k-space: The theorem compares the spaces of continuous functions on $K$ and $L$.
concepts.c:homeomorphism: A homeomorphism is what the isometry produces and what composition uses.
concepts.c:extreme-point: Extreme points of the dual ball are the point masses that encode $K$.
concepts.c:dirac-measure: Point masses $\pm\delta_k$ are the extreme points of the dual ball.
concepts.c:linear-isometry: The adjoint of a surjective linear isometry preserves extreme points.

source.note: The extreme point argument of Arens and Kelley, Characterizations of the space of continuous functions over a compact Hausdorff space, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 62 (1947).

statement: Let a [CW complex](c:cw-complex) $X$ be the union of subcomplexes $A$ and $B$ with $C = A \cap B$ nonempty and connected. If $(A,C)$ is $m$-connected and $(B,C)$ is $n$-connected, $m, n \ge 0$, then $\pi_i(A,C) \to \pi_i(X,B)$ is an isomorphism for $i < m+n$ and a surjection for $i = m+n$.

hypotheses.text: The [CW complex](c:cw-complex) $X$ is the union of subcomplexes $A$ and $B$, and $C = A \cap B$ is nonempty and connected.
The pair $(A, C)$ is $m$-connected, with $m \ge 0$.
The pair $(B, C)$ is $n$-connected, with $n \ge 0$.

conclusion: The map $\pi_i(A,C) \to \pi_i(X,B)$ of [relative homotopy groups](c:relative-homotopy-group) is an isomorphism for $i < m+n$ and a surjection for $i = m+n$.

proofs.name: Cells and general position
proofs.slogan: Reduce to one cell on each side of the pair, then deform maps of disks by general position, where the dimension count gives the range.
proofs.scope: The CW triad form (homotopy excision); the version for homotopy pushouts is another member of the family. The steps outline the geometric proof of the cited text and rest on it for the deformation argument.

roles.why: The subcomplex structure lets one attach cells to $C$ and compare $(A,C)$ with $(X,B)$.
The connectivity $m$ means that $A$ needs only cells of dimension greater than $m$ over $C$.
The connectivity $n$ means that $B$ needs only cells of dimension greater than $n$ over $C$, which fixes the range.

steps.slogan: Replace $A$ and $B$ by complexes built from $C$ with only high-dimensional cells.
steps.detail: Since $(A,C)$ is $m$-connected, relative CW approximation lets us assume that $A$ is obtained from $C$ by [attaching cells](c:attach-cells) of dimension greater than $m$. In the same way $B$ comes from $C$ with cells of dimension greater than $n$. This changes no homotopy group of the pairs in question.

steps.slogan: Reduce to one attached cell on each side by compactness and induction over the cells.
steps.detail: A map of a disk or a sphere meets only finitely many cells, so only finitely many cells matter. Induction on the number of cells then reduces the theorem to $A = C \cup e^k$ and $B = C \cup e^l$ with $k > m$ and $l > n$.

steps.slogan: View $(X, B)$ as $(A, C)$ with the attaching map pushed forward from $C$ into $B$.
steps.detail: In the one-cell case $X = B \cup_C A = B \cup e^k$ is obtained from $B$ by the same cell that $A$ has over $C$. So the map $\pi_i(A,C) \to \pi_i(X,B)$ compares the two pairs of relative homotopy groups of this cell.

steps.slogan: Deform maps of disks into general position with respect to the two cells.
steps.detail: The cited proof represents a class of $\pi_i(X,B)$ by a map of a disk. It uses simplicial approximation and general position, as in Blakers and Massey, to deform that map into $A$ with boundary in $C$. The connectivity of the two pairs supplies the room for these deformations; Hatcher gives them in Section 4.2.

steps.slogan: Count dimensions to get an isomorphism for $i < m+n$ and a surjection for $i = m+n$.
steps.detail: With $k \ge m+1$ and $l \ge n+1$ the deformation of an $i$-disk exists for $i \le m+n$, which gives surjectivity. A homotopy between two such maps is an $(i+1)$-disk, which exists for $i+1 \le m+n$. This gives injectivity for $i < m+n$.

concepts.c:cw-complex: The decomposition into subcomplexes lets cells be attached and counted.
concepts.c:connectivity: Connectivity of the two pairs sets the dimensions of the needed cells.
concepts.c:relative-homotopy-group: The theorem compares relative homotopy groups of $(A,C)$ and $(X,B)$.
concepts.c:attach-cells: The reduction builds $A$ and $B$ from $C$ by attaching high cells.

source.ref: A. Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Cambridge University Press, 2002, Section 4.2 (Theorem 4.23)
source.note: Hatcher proves the CW triad form by the cell reductions and the general position argument of Blakers and Massey (Ann. of Math. 1951).
